summary:
Beyond Earth is a free, interactive web exhibit that tells the story of the machines NASA has left on the Moon and Mars. It is written for school-age space enthusiasts, ages 8–16.
What we developed: An exhibit of 10 machines: Apollo’s lunar module, science stations, laser mirrors and lunar rover, plus five Mars rovers, from Sojourner to Perseverance. Each machine has a story in simple words, real NASA photos, a NASA fact table and a clear status label: Still working, Mission ended or Left behind. Kids can compare machines side by side, take apart an interactive rover and lunar-module diagram, explore a timeline from 1969 to 2026, and test themselves with a quiz that awards badges.
How it addresses the challenge: It introduces young people to NASA’s left-behind hardware and the science it made possible, using NASA mission pages, the NASA Image and Video Library and NASA archives. Every machine page links to its NASA sources.
Why it matters: It shows kids that missions end but their discoveries last. It builds trust by linking claims to NASA, and it works in a web browser with no account.
details:
What it does and how it works
Beyond Earth is a free, interactive website that tells the story of the machines NASA left on the Moon and Mars, written for ages 8–16. It has 10 machine profiles: Apollo’s lunar module, science stations, laser mirrors and rover, plus Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity and Perseverance. Each profile has a story “in simple words”, real NASA photos with credits, and a NASA fact table. Each also has a status label (Still working, Mission ended or Left behind) and links to its NASA sources. Kids can also:

  • Explore a 1969–2026 timeline.
  • Compare machines side by side.
  • Take apart an interactive Mars rover and lunar-module diagram.
  • Take a quiz and earn badges.

The mission text is stored in the site, so it still works if NASA’s image service is slow. A “load more images” button asks NASA’s public Image API for extra photos.

Benefits and intended impact
Young people learn what these machines did, which are still working, and that missions end while their discoveries last. The exhibit is free, needs no account, and runs in a normal browser. We hope it makes NASA’s left-behind hardware feel like a story kids can follow and check for themselves.

Tools and technology
The site is a Next.js and TypeScript web app hosted on Vercel, tested in Microsoft Edge on a personal computer. It uses NASA’s Image and Video Library API for extra photos, and SVG drawings for the anatomy diagrams. An AI coding assistant helped write the website code and the SVG diagrams, and helped draft the student wording. The idea, the choice of machines and the project’s direction are mine.

How it is creative

  • Moving particle models of the Moon, Mars and a rover react to the cursor.
  • Each page keeps the child’s story and NASA’s own fact table side by side.
  • Honest status labels teach that “mission ended” is a normal result.
  • The compare pages highlight teaching points, not scores.
  • The anatomy page has a switch between a solar-powered and a nuclear-powered rover.
  • Collectible badges reward exploring.

Factors we considered

  • Audience: plain language, short paragraphs and a kid-friendly quiz.
  • Accuracy: facts come from NASA pages that are linked on each machine, and active rovers carry an “as of November 2026” note.
  • Honesty: the site says it is not an official NASA website and uses no NASA logos. Sources and AI use are disclosed, and the anatomy drawings are marked as AI-generated.
  • Privacy: no account, and badges stay in the visitor’s browser.
  • Scope: the exhibit covers the Moon and Mars only, and deep-space probes such as Voyager are left out on purpose.
